title: Breakfast by the Sea and Peter Restored

verses.text: Later, by the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus again revealed Himself to the disciples. He made Himself known in this way:
Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael from Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two other disciples were together.
Simon Peter told them, "I am going fishing." "We will go with you," they said. So they went out and got into the boat, but caught nothing that night.
Early in the morning, Jesus stood on the shore, but the disciples did not recognize that it was Jesus.
So He called out to them, "Children, do you have any fish?" "No," they answered.
He told them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." So they cast it there, and they were unable to haul it in because of the great number of fish.
Then the disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, "It is the Lord!" As soon as Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment (for he had removed it) and jumped into the sea.
The other disciples came ashore in the boat. They dragged in the net full of fish, for they were not far from land, only about a hundred yards.
When they landed, they saw a charcoal fire there with fish on it, and some bread.
Jesus told them, "Bring some of the fish you have just caught."
So Simon Peter went aboard and dragged the net ashore. It was full of large fish, 153, but even with so many, the net was not torn.
"Come, have breakfast," Jesus said to them. None of the disciples dared to ask Him, "Who are You?" They knew it was the Lord.
Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish.
This was now the third time that Jesus appeared to the disciples after He was raised from the dead.
When they had finished eating, Jesus asked Simon Peter, "Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?" "Yes, Lord," he answered, "You know I love You." Jesus replied, "Feed My lambs."
Jesus asked a second time, "Simon son of John, do you love Me?" "Yes, Lord," he answered, "You know I love You." Jesus told him, "Shepherd My sheep."

Jesus asked a third time, "Simon son of John, do you love Me?" Peter was deeply hurt that Jesus had asked him a third time, "Do you love Me?" "Lord, You know all things," he replied. "You know I love You." Jesus said to him, "Feed My sheep.

Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go."
Jesus said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. And after He had said this, He told him, "Follow Me."
Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them. He was the one who had leaned back against Jesus at the supper to ask, "Lord, who is going to betray You?"
When Peter saw him, he asked, "Lord, what about him?"
Jesus answered, "If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you? You follow Me!"

Because of this, the rumor spread among the brothers that this disciple would not die. However, Jesus did not say that he would not die, but only, "If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?"
This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down. And we know that his testimony is true.
There are many more things that Jesus did. If all of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself would have space for the books that would be written.

context.author: Traditionally the apostle John
context.genre: Historical narrative — an epilogue that closes the Gospel with a restored Peter, a clarification about the beloved disciple, and a final testimony about the book's author
context.audience: A broad, likely mixed Jewish and Gentile readership toward the end of the first century
context.setting: The scene moves from Jerusalem back to Galilee, to the shore of the Sea of Tiberias (another name for the Sea of Galilee), where several of the disciples had been fishermen. The shoreline is only about a hundred yards from the boat when the miraculous catch is dragged in.
context.custom: Night was the usual time for net-fishing on the lake, which explains why the disciples worked through the dark and came ashore at dawn with nothing. A well-preserved first-century fishing boat found near Kibbutz Ginosar in 1986 shows the size and construction of vessels like theirs. Shared meals were a central sign of fellowship, so Jesus serving bread and fish is both practical hospitality and a deliberate gesture.
context.timelineImmediate: John closes with a final episode set some time after the appearances in Jerusalem, in Galilee. John counts this as the third time Jesus appeared to the disciples as a group: a morning scene of failure turned to abundance, a seaside breakfast, a three-fold conversation with Peter, and a short exchange about the beloved disciple's future.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' three questions to Peter by a charcoal fire deliberately echo Peter's three denials by another charcoal fire in chapter 18. Only two charcoal fires appear in all of John's Gospel: one in the courtyard of denial (18:18) and this one on the beach (21:9). The commission to feed and shepherd the sheep draws on the shepherd imagery of John 10 and Ezekiel 34.
context.sparkNotes: Seven disciples go fishing in Galilee and catch nothing all night, until a stranger on the shore tells them to cast on the right side; the net fills with 153 large fish, and the beloved disciple recognizes the Lord. Jesus feeds them breakfast on the beach beside a charcoal fire, then asks Peter three times, "Do you love Me?" — matching his three denials — each time answering Peter's "yes" with a charge to feed or shepherd His sheep. After predicting the kind of death Peter will face, Jesus declines to answer Peter's question about John with anything more than "You follow Me!" The Gospel ends with a testimony that the disciple who wrote these things is trustworthy, and the observation that the world could not contain all the books if everything Jesus did were written.

translation.meaning: Jesus' first two questions use agapaō, while His third uses phileō, and Peter answers with phileō each time. Some readers find a deliberate shift in the kinds of love here; others think John simply varies his vocabulary for style, as he does elsewhere. Either way, the repetition is plain: three questions answering three denials.

The verb means to tend or shepherd a flock, not just feed it. Jesus' charge to Peter uses the same shepherd imagery He applied to Himself in chapter 10, handing Peter a part in caring for what belongs to Jesus.

A rare word, used in John only twice — here and in 18:18, where Peter stood warming himself while denying Jesus. John gives no comment, but the repeated word invites the reader to hear the second scene against the first.

otBackground.note: God promising to seek out His scattered sheep and tend them Himself — the background to Jesus handing the care of His flock to Peter.
"The LORD is my shepherd" — the most familiar Old Testament picture behind the shepherd language of this chapter.
The wider Scriptural pattern of God commissioning one person for the sake of many, often cited when readers reflect on Peter's commission.

mapCoords.placeName: Shore of the Sea of Tiberias (Galilee)

commentary.note: Henry lays out three ways to read Jesus' "do you love Me more than these?": more than you love these people (James, John, Andrew), more than these boats and nets, or more than these other disciples love Me. On the last, he sees a pointed reminder of Peter's earlier boast, "though all men should deny thee, yet will not I." He notes Jesus drops the comparison in the second and third questions because Peter modestly left it out of his own answer.

The church father Jerome, writing on Ezekiel 47, reports that ancient writers on natural history counted 153 kinds of fish — and read John's number as meaning the apostles' catch took in every kind, a picture of the gospel reaching all types of people. Modern scholar D. A. Carson takes a more cautious line: if John intended symbolism with 153, he has hidden it well.

Ellicott reads the exact figure as a mark of firsthand memory rather than a code: the fish were all "great," so their size and number led to an exact tally being taken, which "would be talked of among the Apostles and their friends and fellow-craftsmen" and is recorded with "the picturesque exactness which is characteristic of St. John."

overview.summary: Seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing until Jesus tells them to cast on the right side. On the shore He cooks breakfast, asks Peter three times if he loves Him, and tells him to feed His sheep.
overview.settingLine: The shore of the Sea of Tiberias.

history.t: Herod Antipas named his capital for the emperor Tiberius, so the lake took the Roman name.
Jesus hints at Peter's death, and early tradition says he was martyred under Rome.

customs.t: Galilean fishermen worked at night, using nets let down from boats.
Bread and fish were the staple meal of the lakeshore.

archaeology.t: A first-century fishing boat was found in the lake in 1986.
A church beside the lake honors the breakfast Jesus served.

overview.discussion: Jesus asked Peter three times, "Do you love me?" Why might He ask the same thing again and again?
overview.book: The fourth Gospel · 21 chapters. Written so readers would believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.
overview.author: John
